prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock
for the discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductors

statement.case_for: My opening ballot put spherical-aberration correction first, but reading the other seven ballots changes what I think the committee can defend. The optical lattice clock is the only shortlisted candidate that every member ranked, and it fits the mandate as I read it: an invention (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, 2001-2003) turned into a measurement (Ye's strontium clocks near 1e-18) that several independent laboratories now reproduce and compare routinely. The original proposal and the demonstration are by identifiable people, and the two credited names map onto them without a large collaboration to disentangle. Pairing it with Hosono's 2008 discovery of superconductivity in fluorine-doped LaFeAsO gives a second, clearly separate achievement: an original experimental observation by one group, reproduced within months worldwide, with a clean attribution. This is a discovery in condensed matter alongside an invention in precision measurement, three people in total, and both parts are experimentally verified and mature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that I am setting aside the candidate I ranked first. Aberration correction (B046) removed a limit standing since Scherzer's 1936 theorem and is, in my view, a tool that opened a door, but only I ranked it, the credited names omit Ondrej Krivanek, and I cannot be absolutely sure from the supplied credit that Rose, Haider and Urban are the right set. Against my chosen pairing: the lattice clock sits close to the 2005 frequency-comb prize and to ion-clock work (Wineland's group), so a committee could regard it as a refinement of recognised precision spectroscopy rather than an original door; the redefinition of the second has not yet happened; and Hosono has only three supporters, with Tc subsequently raised by other groups and the pairing mechanism still unexplained, so some colleagues will say the discovery is clean but the physics is unfinished.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B018) first, valuing the opening of a new observational window, and considers Halzen and Karle a fair, compact credit despite a collaboration of several hundred and DUMAND/AMANDA predecessors.
responses.response: I share the value of a new window, and I ranked B018 fourth. Where I differ is on attribution, which is the point I would not compromise on: the committee must be sure that the people credited did the original work. With a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA, and DUMAND before it, I cannot see yet that two names capture the first detection, and the source-level associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are weaker than the diffuse flux. I would like Mark to say concretely what Karle and Halzen each did that others did not. Until that is clear I prefer a candidate where the original work is traceable to named people. I note that Pearce ranked the clock second, so we may agree on B040 even if not on first place.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Toner-Tu-Vicsek active-matter theory first, citing a simple general mechanism and the long-range order that defies Mermin-Wagner, but concedes that experimental confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is partial. He ranks the topological insulators second and flags that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are omitted.
responses.response: Bernhard's own caveat on B008 is the reason I cannot support it as first choice. The Prize is for a result verified in experiment, and agreement of the measured exponents with the theory is only partial, so the verification is stronger for the qualitative phase than for the theory credited. On B061 I agree that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a serious problem, perhaps more than a footnote: the HgTe experiment by Molenkamp followed their proposal, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio does not obviously reflect who did the original work. I would want the committee to settle that before this goes forward, and the 2016 overlap needs a clear answer too. I do not dispute the scientific importance, only whether the credit as supplied is right.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the CMB acoustic-peak mapping (B023) first, arguing that the WMAP trio is coherent and that it turned cosmology into a precision science, while admitting that Puget, Sunyaev and the balloon experiments are a real allocation problem.
responses.response: I accept the importance of the measurement, and it is clearly mature. My concern is the one Ulf raises himself: with Planck, the balloon experiments and Sunyaev's theory all having claims, three names from WMAP alone may not identify who first resolved the peaks, and the COBE prize in 2006 and the 2019 cosmology prize already sit nearby. As the only member ranking this candidate, he would need to show that the original experiment, not the later and more precise one, is the one credited. I would not set it against the clock on merit, but I do not find the attribution settled.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the optical lattice clock as an original invention distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and from ion clocks, and whether it prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether Hosono alone is sufficient for the iron-based superconductors, given that the early Tc increases came from other groups, and whether the unexplained pairing mechanism weakens the case.
Whether Ondrej Krivanek's STEM aberration-corrector work must be credited alongside Rose, Haider and Urban, which determines whether B046 can be put forward at all.
I have not seen the full detail of colleagues' views on the IceCube credit or on the quantum-information candidates; some of my responses rely on the summaries in the ballots.
statement.conflict_note: I am an electron microscopist and head of a division at Chalmers, and B046 (aberration-corrected TEM) is in my own field. My profile records no personal tie to Rose, Urban or Haider, but my professional proximity to the instruments could be seen as a conflict, which is one reason I do not make B046 my preferred part while its attribution is uncertain. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics, though his top candidate is not among my preferred parts. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
